news_items.summary_en: Ancient water clocks were crafted from a variety of materials; those used in royal palaces were made from gold, silver, and jade.
news_items.body: In ancient China, before the advent of mechanical clocks and digital devices, people relied mainly on night watchmen to keep time, prevent fires and maintain their daily routines. But how did the watchmen tell the time? Chinese night watchmen mainly used two methods: clepsydras and incense sticks. A clepsydra, also known as a water clock, measures time through the regulated flow of water from a vessel. The ancient Chinese divided the night into five gengs. Each geng lasted around two hours, though the exact duration varied by season. The first geng usually ran from 7pm to 9pm, while the fifth and final geng ended around 5am. The campaign stop marked Trump’s second in the state in as many weeks, an indication of the importance of the Senate contest in Georgia. With less than two weeks until election day on November 3, though, Representative Mike Collins, the Republican candidate, faces an uphill battle in a state that was once a Republican stronghold. Trump is at historic low approval ratings and his efforts to tout manufacturing investment promises have failed to resonate with voters who are more concerned with high costs of living and wage growth. The war in Iran has also spiked energy prices, adding further strain to household budgets. The Audi announcement marks a political win for Trump, who has been on the defensive about the domestic effects of his tariffs, particularly on inflation, in a number of battleground Senate races. news_items.summary_en: ‘I don’t know how much longer I can do this,’ says the stand-up comedian, fresh off three sold-out Hong Kong shows. Is he joking?
news_items.body: “I think about quitting all the time,” says Jordan Leung, known to his Instagram followers as @69ranch. As one of Hong Kong’s most prominent stand-up comedians to emerge in recent years, Leung’s pessimism is surprising. “I don’t wanna make social media content,” the 33-year-old admits. “Now I’m just fixated on likes and stuff … I don’t know how much longer I can do this.” Sitting directly across the table from him, it is not always easy to tell when Leung is being sincere or performing his deadpan jesting – yet, at this moment, his exhaustion sounds genuine. Leung recently returned to Hong Kong from his base in New York, taking a couple of weeks to spend time with family and recover from jet lag ahead of his “Back to Work” tour shows in Whampoa in October. Originally planning to perform one show each in English and Cantonese on October 17 and 18, the comedian added an extra Cantonese show on the final day thanks to overwhelming demand. At his English-language performance, Leung was his usual understated character: clad in black and sporting his signature thick moustache, delivering monotone observations on the bizarre experiences of his daily life. His set included stories of being hit on by a billionaire’s daughter after a gig, childhood memories of realising his uncle is gay and the challenges of touring Japan. He also touched on his life as a full-time stand-up comedian, joking that his mother would have sought an abortion if she had known this was his career choice. Ironically, during our interview, Leung reveals that since finding success in comedy, his parents insist he cannot quit. “‘You’ve spent too much time on this,’” he quotes them. A comedy career pivot Leung grew up in Hong Kong before moving to the United States at 15, then returned to the city in 2020 after getting laid off from a tech job. He has toyed with stand-up comedy since he was 23, taking classes at New York’s renowned Comedy Cellar and performing bar gigs as early as 2017. He always knew he would quit tech and pursue something more creative once he saved enough money anyway. “I knew there was a comedy scene here [in Hong Kong], and I knew I would be able to produce some shows, but I just never imagined the scale that it would eventually become,” Leung says. “But that was probably one of the most important things I did in my career.” He built a significant following through viral Instagram videos making jokes about Hong Kong life using bawdy humour, often amassing hundreds of thousands of views. Eventually, he even held shows at MacPherson Stadium in Mong Kok in 2024. Then, in 2025, Leung returned to the US. His live sets often feature jokes that lean into Asia diaspora experiences, such as learning Hong Kong slang words for intimate body parts. At his recent English live show, Leung delivered several jokes about female genitalia seemingly aimed at a much younger audience than the crowd of 30- and 40-year-olds present – but the crowd guffawed, nonetheless. The response was mixed for a particular joke deriding Shenzhen, with roaring laughter and booing from the audience alike. The gag was in vein with much of his set: “edgy” but not countercultural. Some of the funniest moments came when he switched to Cantonese to make small quips and quick jabs. Following his Cantonese show on October 18, controversy erupted over his opening act, Taiwanese-Hong Kong comedian Shen Jong, whose set included an offensive joke about the benefits of sleeping with female cancer patients. news_items.summary_en: Beijing seeks to safeguard billions in regional infrastructure and economic investments while hewing to its pledge of non-interference.
news_items.body: Chinese President Xi Jinping outlined Beijing’s formula for tackling African conflicts and hot-button issues during a meeting this month with visiting Togolese leader Faure Gnassingbe, framing it around four principles linking peace to development. The principles focus on African-led security free from outside intervention; upholding sovereignty and UN Charter principles; rejecting force and sanctions and favouring ceasefires through dialogue; and focusing on both immediate security concerns and long-term development. Asked last week whether the principles could be applied to northern Ethiopia and the heightened tensions with neighbouring Eritrea, Chinese foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning said they offered “practical guidance” for the Horn of Africa. Days later, a joint statement following a meeting between Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi and his Djiboutian counterpart, Abdoulkader Houssein Omar, said China would continue to play a constructive role in mediating regional disputes through its existing Horn of Africa peace and development initiative, subject to the wishes of the countries concerned. Beijing has financed major infrastructure projects in the region under the Belt and Road Initiative, its China-centred trade and investment scheme. These include the Addis Ababa–Djibouti Standard Gauge Railway, as well as oil, fishing and maritime interests across Sudan, South Sudan, Somalia and Djibouti. Yet, Beijing remains reluctant to intervene directly, opting instead to support African-led diplomacy to preserve its long-standing doctrine of state non-interference. As conflict in Ethiopia’s Tigray region threatens to destabilise the Horn of Africa, China seeks to strike a delicate diplomatic balance, advocating for peaceful, African-led solutions that align with Xi’s conflict-resolution principles. The idea is to safeguard China’s billions in regional infrastructure and economic investments while carefully maintaining its core foreign policy pledge of non-interference. But experts said lasting peace would ultimately depend on regional actors addressing internal factionalism, respecting state sovereignty and fostering inclusive dialogue alongside broader international peace efforts. Yun Sun, a senior fellow and director of the China programme at the Stimson Centre, a Washington-based think tank, said Beijing’s response reflected concern about what renewed fighting could mean for its interests in the Horn of Africa. “I think it first and foremost points out China’s concern and aversion to instability,” Sun said. “War and conflicts fundamentally undermine China’s interests on the ground.” China also faced a diplomatic constraint, she added, saying it sought to influence how conflicts were resolved without abandoning its stated principle of non-interference in other countries’ affairs. news_items.body: Sherry Shum has embraced a new shopping routine after finding a smart vending machine near her home in Chai Wan in Hong Kong. The 37-year-old retail worker uses her phone to scan a QR code, opens the smart machine’s door, picks up a bottle of Coca-Cola, an oolong tea and a pack of potato chips, closes it and walks away with HK$60 (US$7.70) worth of goods. The whole process is so seamless that the bulk of the time is spent deciding what to buy. The moment Shum takes an item from the shelf, the machine detects the product based on its appearance and debits her account. Once she shuts the door, the bill is settled via the payment method she selected before opening it. “I buy things basically every day … I can grab multiple items at once after just opening the door,” she said. “The open-door machines are more convenient because you do not have to wait for items to drop one by one from traditional machines that sometimes get stuck.” Over the decades, vending machines have evolved from simple dispensers of bottled or canned drinks into smart retail points that combine digital payments and data-driven consumer insights. They now offer a low-cost retail channel for third parties such as local charities, selling products like flowers and daily necessities – from disposable underwear to sanitary towels. These artificial intelligence-powered open-door vending machines have been growing in popularity in Shenzhen in the past couple of years, but they remain uncommon in Hong Kong. Some operators have pledged to install more of them across the city in the coming months, with one reporting higher sales revenue during the trial stage. IVM Technology is one of Hong Kong’s largest operators, managing about 800 AI vending machines alongside 1,500 traditional ones in Hong Kong, the firm’s founder and managing director Leo Lui told the South China Morning Post. Hong Kong had an estimated 15,000 to 17,000 vending machines, with the number expected to increase as the lower capital costs of AI machines attract new market entrants, Lui said. “It will not surprise me if there are 30,000 to 40,000 machines later,” he said. Lui pointed to Hong Kong’s exorbitant logistics, labour and parking costs – such as paying HK$200 just to park a delivery van for restocking at major commercial sites – as a major bottleneck. Unlike mainland Chinese operators who could rely on low delivery expenses to sell low-margin goods, Hong Kong vending businesses faced fixed transport costs of about HK$2 per item, forcing them to focus on higher-priced, premium inventory, Lui said. While the new open-door models generated 20 to 30 per cent more revenue in closed environments such as offices, traditional machines still outperformed them by 30 per cent in transient public spaces like bus stops, Lui explained. “On the streets, some consumers might find the new machines are too slow, whereas with an Octopus card on a traditional machine, the product drops in a second after a purchase is made,” he said. news_items.summary_en: Even as the region’s economic downturn is expected to worsen, Gulf states are slated to spend tens of billions of dollars on infrastructure.

Their hydrocarbon-fuelled economies were glitzy oases of growth, inoculated from the conflict in Gaza that had rocked other parts of the Middle East for several years. Underpinned by decades-old US security guarantees and conflict mediation by billionaire sheikhs, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Qatar cultivated images as peaceful lands of opportunity as they invested staggering amounts of money in economic diversification programmes. Backed by sovereign wealth funds with trillions of dollars invested mostly in the West, these leading states of the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) embarked on transformative programmes to reposition their economies amid the global transition away from oil and gas. Similar diversification initiatives were also happening in Kuwait, Oman and Bahrain, the other three GCC members. Such a shift towards long-term economic stability is important in maintaining the political legitimacy of the Gulf monarchies in the eyes of their burgeoning young populations, especially amid mounting public anger at the carnage in Gaza, according to analysts. The GCC states, as well as other Muslim-majority governments such as Pakistan and Turkey, eventually persuaded US President Donald Trump to end the Gaza war in October 2025, renewing optimism about the Gulf economies. However, everything changed soon after the Gaza ceasefire, when Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu managed to convince Trump to go to war against Iran. Rather than just retaliating against Israel, Iran has also vented its fury against the GCC states, attacking energy infrastructure, airports and ships sailing through the Strait of Hormuz. With Trump weighing his options, including both another military escalation and a politically inconclusive end to the war with Iran after midterm congressional elections on November 5, uncertainty reigns in the Gulf region. The eruption of war between Saudi Arabia and Tehran’s Houthi rebel allies in Yemen last month has exacerbated these anxieties. In the second quarter of this year, Saudi Arabia’s economy – the largest in the GCC – fell by 4.8 per cent from 3 per cent growth in the first quarter. The UAE’s economy – the Gulf’s logistical hub – decreased by 2.1 per cent from an expansion of 3 per cent over the same period. Qatar’s economic outlook worsened, with its GDP declining by 15.7 per cent in the second quarter, accelerating from a drop of 7 per cent in the first quarter. news_items.summary_en: Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said the government would explore nuclear power and boost global partnerships for energy security.
news_items.body: Singapore expects all parties who have signed commercial contracts for gas supplies to “honour their commitments”, said Prime Minister Lawrence Wong on Sunday after Indonesia cut its exports. Indonesia began reducing natural gas exports to Singapore on Saturday. Indonesia’s upstream oil and gas regulator SKK Migas said the move was to divert more supplies to domestic electricity needs. Singapore’s Energy Market Authority said the reduction of 31 million standard cubic feet of gas a day amounts to less than 2 per cent of Singapore’s total daily gas demand. About 95 per cent of Singapore’s electricity is generated using natural gas and it imports a significant amount of this gas through pipelines from Indonesia. “The gas supplies are covered by commercial contracts. We expect all parties to honour their commitments and Singapore’s gas importer will take the necessary steps to protect its rights and interests under these contracts,” Wong said. Singapore has been readying itself for such risks, the prime minister added. It has invested in liquefied natural gas (LNG) terminals to import natural gas from different countries, without having to rely on pipelines, providing more options to manage any disruptions to supply. However, Singapore must look beyond natural gas to cleaner sources of power that can provide reliable electricity around the clock, Wong added. This is why authorities are studying the potential of nuclear energy, he said. “Understandably, there are concerns about the safety of nuclear power in a small and densely populated country like Singapore. We take the concerns very seriously. Safety must come first,” Wong said. “But we should not rule out an option simply because it is difficult or controversial. We must assess the risks and trade-offs carefully, engage Singaporeans, and eventually make the right decision to secure our energy future.” From 2027, Singapore will be embarking on an assessment by the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) to gauge the country’s ability to make an informed decision on adopting nuclear energy. Known as the IAEA’s Integrated Nuclear Infrastructure Review, each phase comes with key milestones that have to be reached to guide countries in their understanding of the commitments and obligations associated with developing a nuclear power programme. news_items.title_en: ‘Mum, good’: Chinese woman wakes vegetative daughter-in-law after 17 years of care | South China Morning Post
news_items.summary_en: Xuan feeds Xu liquid food spoonful by spoonful, taking an hour per meal, and turns her over 10 times daily to prevent bedsores.
news_items.body: A woman in eastern China has been devotedly caring for her daughter-in-law for 17 years, ever since she fell into a vegetative state, moving social media users. The younger woman, surnamed Xu, fell into a vegetative state in 2009 after being struck by a truck in her village in Qingyun county, Shandong province. The accident happened just one month after she got married, Shandian News reported. Since then, her mother-in-law, Xuan Fengying, has cared for her around the clock. “She married my son, so she’s my child. How could I abandon her?” the 68-year-old Xuan was quoted as saying. Xuan fed Xu liquid food one spoonful at a time, and each meal took an hour. She also helped Xu turn over more than 10 times a day to prevent bedsores. Other caregiving tasks included washing Xu after she became incontinent and regularly massaging her muscles. Xuan also talked to Xu about news from the family and their village, played her favourite songs, and repeatedly called her name. Several years ago, Xu miraculously emerged from the vegetative state. Her mother-in-law continued to care for her, as severe brain damage from the accident had left Xu with the cognitive abilities of a four-year-old. Xuan helped Xu learn to walk and take part in other rehabilitation exercises. Xu can now speak a few words and even cook simple meals on her own. “Mum, good,” Xu was filmed saying to her mother-in-law. “I have no other wish than for her to keep getting better. I feel a little relieved that she can cook. That way, after I pass away, she’ll still have something to eat,” Xuan said. “I told my son that if I pass away, he should keep caring for his wife,” Xuan added. She said her legs had ached for years and that she had high blood pressure. Xuan recalled that when Xu once fell to the ground, she had to ask a neighbour to help her get Xu back up. “Of course I envy other people’s leisurely lives. They can go dancing in the squares. But my responsibility is to care for my daughter-in-law,” Xuan said. A flood of comments followed, with many people moved by Xuan’s extraordinary devotion. “Such great maternal love! Salute to this mother-in-law,” one social media user wrote. Another commented: “Wishing this elderly woman good health and a long life.” Stories of people devoting many years to caring for family members often make headlines in China. Earlier this year, a husband in central China’s Henan province won widespread praise online for caring for his severely paraplegic wife for 25 years.

She said it was “unforgivable” for a Chinese person to wear the rising sun flag. Japanese anime began appearing on Chinese television in the 1980s and gradually gained a larger audience over the following decades. According to a 2018 report by Chinese consultancy iResearch, China had more than 200 million online anime users in 2018, with nearly 80 per cent of 803 surveyed anime consumers expressing a preference for Japanese animation. news_items.title_en: Why more Japanese women are choosing ‘silver divorce’ after decades of marriage | South China Morning Post
news_items.summary_en: As children leave home and with changing pension rules, more older Japanese women are choosing to walk away from distant marriages.
news_items.body: Ayumi lives alone in a spacious suburban house originally bought to raise a family, her two cats now her only full-time companions. Her two daughters have grown up and left home, and her husband of more than two decades moved out nearly a year ago as they finalise a divorce. For the 62-year-old Kawasaki resident, who spoke on condition that her surname be withheld, this was not how she envisioned her later years. “He worked very long hours, including on weekends, and I was always busy taking care of the house and raising the children,” Ayumi said. “I think we worked well as a team at the beginning, but somewhere along the way, we just stopped talking like we had before.” The marriage had its fair share of ups and downs – financial stress during their daughters’ university years and the deaths of their respective parents. But the final break came when the girls left home. “It felt like we were almost strangers with nothing in common,” she said. “Before, we had always put our children first. But suddenly they had their own lives, and we both realised there was not much holding us together any more.” Ayumi’s experience reflects a growing trend across Japan. While total divorces nationwide have steadily declined since peaking in the early 2000s, separations among couples married for 20 years or longer – commonly called “silver divorce” – continue to rise. Data from the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare released in September showed that such late-life break-ups reached a record 24.2 per cent in 2025, rising 0.4 percentage points from the previous year. The total number of divorces in 2025, however, fell to 179,073, down 6,831 from 185,904 in 2024. Financial independence Several changes have caused older women to re-evaluate unhappy or distant marriages later in life. Sumie Kawakami, a lecturer at Yamanashi Gakuin University and author of a book on gender issues, said an “empty nest” frequently exposed deep emotional divides built up over decades. “Many find that they had grown a long way apart during the years of raising their children,” Kawakami said. This has been exacerbated by more women entering employment, earning a wage that gives a degree of self-sufficiency previous generations lacked. A key turning point was Japan’s 2007 pension system reform, which allowed divorced spouses to claim up to 50 per cent of the Employees’ Pension Insurance contributions accumulated by their partner during the marriage. “For women earning less than 1.3 million yen [US$8,217] a year, this was significant,” Kawakami said, as it provided a financial safety net upon retirement that previously did not exist. Married, but living apart Japan’s demanding corporate culture also plays a key role long before divorce papers are filed. Under the common practice of tanshin funin (solo work transfers), companies can relocate married male employees to distant domestic or overseas offices for years at a time. Wives often stay behind so children do not have to change schools. “These situations can go on for decades,” Kawakami said. “One of my friends never actually lived in the house he bought for his family; his wife and children live there and he visits when he can. So it is not at all surprising that when the husband reaches retirement age he has nothing in common any more with his wife.” The price of silence Beyond the legal and financial costs, late-life separation can carry a distinct psychological burden. news_items.title_en: Opinion | Hong Kong needs a civil service fit for a changed world | South China Morning Post
news_items.summary_en: Beyond administrative expertise, civil servants must now master technology, cross-departmental cooperation and strategic flexibility.
news_items.body: Hong Kong’s civil service has long enjoyed a reputation for efficiency, professionalism and probity. It has also been a pillar of stability, particularly during the transition from British to Chinese rule. Outside the general and administrative grades, many civil servants spend much of their careers in relatively specialised areas of responsibility. This allows them to develop deep expertise and makes them dependable regulators and administrators. However, it can also make it harder to adapt when new challenges cut across established departmental boundaries. Recent events have put this model under scrutiny. The fire that engulfed Wang Fuk Court in Tai Po last November, claiming 168 lives and destroying more than a thousand homes, raised grave questions about building safety and regulatory oversight. Subsequent construction scandals involving luxury homes and public housing estates, together with concerns over lift installations at a major public hospital and in numerous other buildings, have further tested public confidence in the government. Hong Kong was once a British outpost built on trade. Government played a relatively limited role in economic development, while free trade, market forces and the city’s strategic position at the crossroads of East and West helped it prosper. The city continues to be recognised internationally for its economic freedom. That said, the experience since 1997 has shown that free markets cannot address every economic and social challenge. Following the handover, the 1997-98 Asian financial crisis and the outbreak of severe acute respiratory syndrome dealt severe blows to the economy. Then-chief executive Tung Chee-hwa sought to revive growth through initiatives including Hong Kong Disneyland and the development of a cruise terminal. A substantial relaxation of travel arrangements for mainland residents subsequently helped tourism and the wider economy recover. The lesson is not that government should replace market forces, but that it must be capable of responding decisively when circumstances change. Hong Kong’s comparatively small economy is increasingly intertwined with a mainland economy undergoing rapid technological transformation. China’s strategic competition with the United States is likely to shape the global economic and technological landscape for years to come. Beijing has made the development of “new quality productive forces” a key national priority. For Hong Kong, the implications are substantial. The need to harness technology, develop new industries and improve productivity features prominently in the national development agenda and the city’s own planning priorities. The challenge is to translate these ambitions into effective policies, an enabling regulatory environment and tangible economic gains. Civil servants have already had to navigate a growing range of emerging technologies and business models. These include mobile payments, ride-hailing, autonomous driving, the low-altitude economy, green maritime fuel, sustainable aviation fuel and hydrogen as an alternative energy source. Each presents regulatory questions that existing rules might not adequately address. Artificial intelligence (AI) presents perhaps the greatest test. The government has committed substantial resources to AI research and development, including support for universities and the expansion of computing infrastructure. A proposed data centre in the Northern Metropolis is expected to increase Hong Kong’s computing capacity substantially. Investment in infrastructure is only part of the equation. news_items.body: Hong Kong schools handled an average of 496 bullying cases each academic year from 2022 to 2025 – a 32 per cent jump compared with the previous three years, according to the Education Bureau. A youth group attributed the increase to greater reporting driven by heightened mental health awareness, but also students struggling to distinguish playful jokes from bullying. According to the bureau, public primary and secondary schools recorded an average of 496 bullying cases each year between 2022 and 2025, up 32 per cent from the 377 recorded annually from 2019 to 2022. The bureau told the Legislative Council in 2023 that the number of cases involving school bullying, including cyberbullying, from the 2019-20 to 2021-22 school years was 411, 306 and 413 respectively. The average number for these three school years was 377. The figures were based on information contained in the bureau’s annual questionnaire surveys on guidance and discipline cases in schools. The bureau did not provide any annual breakdown for the years between 2022 and 2025. It said the data for the current school year was still being compiled. “The number of student cases involving school bullying, including cyberbullying, handled by schools averaged 496 per year between the 2022–23 and 2024–25 school years, with the annual figures remaining generally stable,” a bureau spokesman said. But he said comparing the two sets of figures for 2019–22 and 2022–25 might not be appropriate, as the first triennium was marked by the Covid pandemic, during which students attended some classes online. Last month, the Programme for International Student Assessment, a worldwide study of 15-year-olds’ learning and education by the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) revealed that 22.2 per cent of students in Hong Kong aged 15 reported experiencing some form of bullying at least a few times a month. The city’s overall figure was higher than the OECD average of 19.6 per cent. Hong Kong ranked 32nd among the 86 surveyed countries and cities, including ones that were not members of the organisation. The Hong Kong Federation of Youth Groups has been commissioned by the bureau to provide advice and counselling services on peer conflict management to students and parents at all primary and secondary schools this academic year. The group also has social workers stationed in 59 primary and secondary schools. Andy Chan Ying-kit, head of service at the youth group, partly attributed the rise in bullying cases to greater public concern driven by increased awareness of student mental health. “Some research indicates mental health issues related to bullying cases lead to emotional distress and social withdrawal,” he said. Chan added that younger generations often struggled to distinguish playful joking from bullying, such as creating altered images targeting victims or repeatedly kicking classmates out of chat groups. He said resolving cases had become significantly more difficult with some students airing their grievances on social media and drawing comments from other online users. “The victim faces severe public scrutiny and media pressure, making mediated resolutions far harder to achieve,” he said. Chan noted that some cases became more complicated because victims might turn into bullies themselves when seeking revenge, making it harder for teachers and social workers to determine fault or mediate effectively. He said parents were also paying much closer attention to their children’s well-being, and their dissatisfaction with how schools handled cases often led to confrontation with administrators. Parents should prioritise their children’s emotional well-being instead of prematurely escalating the situation, he advised. “Focus first on comforting your child, listening to their feelings and addressing their mental health. news_items.title_en: Sri Lanka’s property boom gives Chinese developers hope. But familiar risks linger | South China Morning Post
news_items.summary_en: Colombo’s luxury property rally is drawing fresh interest from Chinese-backed developments, but analysts warn against speculative excess.
news_items.body: A Chinese developer behind one of Sri Lanka’s biggest projects has reason to celebrate as a luxury property boom lifts sentiment in the South Asian nation and fuels optimism about the market’s prospects. Analysts, however, cautioned that a string of disappointing Chinese overseas property investments over the past decade underlined the risks of speculative excess that could lead to a boom-to-bust scenario, particularly in a country where regulation remained uneven. “Chinese developers, having already learned a hard lesson from the property market [slump in China], need to stay cautious,” said Wang Feng, chairman of Shanghai-based financial services group Ye Lang Capital. “I bet they won’t get carried away by the recent price surge in Sri Lanka because of their high risk-awareness.” Three new luxury residential projects in Colombo Port City – a landmark development built on reclaimed land by China Harbour Engineering Co (Chec) and the Sri Lankan government – had drawn strong interest from local buyers attracted by projections of substantial investment returns, according to a report by online magazine The Diplomat. The three developments, built by Sri Lanka’s top real estate firms, represent a combined investment of US$650 million. Developers had marketed the developments with projected returns of up to 100 per cent over four years, according to the report. Colombo Port City itself is a US$1.4 billion development being built by Chec, a unit of Chinese multinational engineering and construction company China Communications Construction. Construction began in September 2014 and it was described by China’s State-owned Assets Supervision and Administration Commission as the largest foreign direct investment-backed infrastructure project in Sri Lanka at the time. The reclaimed land was envisioned to create a new central business district focused on tourism, financial services and logistics, eventually attracting 280,000 residents and workers, according to the state-assets regulator. In May, Chec held a topping-out ceremony for an affordable public housing project in Colombo that is expected to deliver an initial 112 homes for low-income residents, with a further 1,884 units planned. A survey by Sri Lanka’s central bank found that more than 20 per cent of flats were bought for investment purposes in the first quarter of 2026, while developers continued to shift to higher-end projects to capitalise on rising demand. About 52 per cent of home sales in the three months ended March were priced above 50 million rupees (US$150,600), up from 33 per cent a year earlier, according to the survey. Sri Lanka is among the countries participating in China’s Belt and Road Initiative, launched by President Xi Jinping in 2013 to strengthen trade and infrastructure links across Asia, Africa, Europe and beyond. Despite the optimism, questions remain about market oversight. According to The Diplomat, Sri Lanka’s Condominium Management Authority oversees the country’s luxury homes. But its main responsibility lies in monitoring and supervising completed buildings, and it has limited ability to regulate the fast-moving presale home market, where speculative capital has poured into projects. Chinese developers’ go-global drive over the past decade has also produced mixed results, particularly after Beijing tightened controls on capital outflows and China’s domestic property crisis undermined financing conditions. One of the highest-profile examples was developer Country Garden’s US$100 billion Forest City project in Johor, Malaysia, which was launched in 2016 to house 700,000 people in a sprawling development of condominium complexes, office towers, hotels, malls and schools. Yet by 2020, the project was home to only about 9,000 people, despite the sale of 28,000 units during its first phase. The challenges facing some Chinese investments in Sri Lanka have also persisted. news_items.title_en: Singapore embraces AI for cyber defence, with one caveat: breach transparency | South China Morning Post
news_items.summary_en: The city state will take a ‘pragmatic’ approach to AI adoption as it seeks to bolster protection for its critical infrastructure.
news_items.body: Singapore is turning to major technology firms to strengthen its cyber defences, even as it presses them for greater transparency over security breaches – a balancing act facing regional governments as they seek to harness artificial intelligence while guarding against the risks it introduces. Those risks were highlighted by an AI agent linked to OpenAI that gained unauthorised access to files on an Australian government website earlier this year, raising questions over how quickly companies disclose security incidents as AI systems become more capable and autonomous. At a summit earlier this month, Singapore launched a refreshed cybersecurity strategy that would see it progressively deploy AI across its cyber defence operations and work with industry partners to accelerate adoption, as it seeks to bolster protection for its critical infrastructure. The city state would take a “pragmatic” approach to AI adoption, allowing it to choose between the “best available” models, K. Shanmugam, coordinating minister for national security, said during a speech at Singapore International Cyber Week on October 13. “We will not need to develop our own AI models for every use case. What we really need is the capability to evaluate the best available models and to adapt them to our own needs.” Anthropic’s Claude is among the models Singapore is exploring as it seeks to strengthen its cyber defences. The US technology firm signed an agreement with Singapore on the sidelines of the summit, setting out areas of AI cooperation, including safety, security, responsible adoption and research into the impact of adoption. “Singapore has been a leader in responsible AI, with a long track record of investment in model testing and evaluation,” said Anthropic co-founder Benjamin Mann at the signing on October 13, a day before the firm opened its fifth Asia-Pacific office in the city state. Anthropic already has offices in Japan, India, South Korea and Australia. “With this [memorandum of understanding], we’ll partner with Singapore to help ensure the transition to powerful AI goes well here, across Asia-Pacific, and around the world,” Mann said. Safety and transparency concerns The partnerships offer governments access to emerging technologies and technical expertise, but also make transparency and oversight increasingly important as AI systems become more capable and autonomous. On the sidelines of the event, Shanmugam told the media that Singapore had sought greater transparency from major technology companies, following meetings with firms including Anthropic, Google, Amazon and OpenAI. “They need to notify us early on when something happens, taking a leaf from the experience in Australia and what happened there,” he said. “Generally, the companies have expressed an attitude of cooperation. But I would say it’s work in progress. It’s something that we are talking to them about.” Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese criticised OpenAI in September over what he called an “unacceptable” breach involving an AI agent that infiltrated a government health website and accessed public and non-public files in June. Albanese accused the firm of taking “way too long” to tell Canberra about the incident. The San Francisco-headquartered company, which said it learned of the breach in August, apologised and acknowledged that its handling of the incident was “not enough”. In July, open-source AI platform Hugging Face said it had been hacked by autonomous AI agents. Less than a week later, OpenAI revealed that the “unprecedented cyber incident” was driven by a combination of its models after it lost control of them during a security test. Singapore had yet to encounter another attack like those attributed to cyberthreat group UNC3886, Shanmugam said. news_items.title_en: Do you have empty nest syndrome? 5 signs – and expert ways to cope | South China Morning Post
news_items.summary_en: Watching your children leave home triggers a wave of mixed emotions. An expert shares how to process the shift and move forward.
news_items.body: If you feel lost or overwhelmed now your children have left the nest, you are far from alone. Many parents experience empty nest syndrome at this time of the year. “Empty nest syndrome isn’t a mental health condition, but a set of feelings or symptoms that parents might feel when all their children have left home,” says Dr Elizabeth Wakeland, consultant, clinical and forensic psychologist at Cygnet Health Care in the UK. “It’s a period of significant life change where parents are trying to figure out who they are and what their life looks like now their children are no longer in the home.” Empty nest symptoms Here are five signs of empty nest syndrome to look out for and advice about how to navigate this period. 1. Sense of grief “Some parents might experience emotions around grief, loss and sadness,” Wakeland says. “Although their children haven’t passed away, there’s still a loss of presence and a change in relationship.” 2. Anxiety “There might also be some feelings of anxiety,” Wakeland says. “Children living outside the home might increase your anxiety because they are no longer with you all the time and you might be worried about their safety.” That anxiety might manifest itself in constant communication. “This anxiety might present in behaviours that are directly related, such as calling or sending messages constantly to check in on your children,” she says. “This is when our involvement, or what people sometimes refer to as ‘helicopter parenting’, might come into play.” 3. Mood changes “As well as these low feelings and a sense of emptiness, there might also be some positive feelings,” Wakeland says. “For example, you might have some excitement about your child moving on and progressing, or some pride in what they are going on to do. “So, it might feel a bit up and down for a while, and a mixture of positive and negative emotions might play out.” This can trigger guilt: “A parent might feel guilt around how they should or shouldn’t feel, or what they should or shouldn’t be doing now that their children have moved out.” 4. Identity crisis “When you become a parent you have to adapt and mould yourself and your life around your children,” Wakeland says. “Children take up a lot of time, energy and thinking, and it becomes a big part of your identity. Therefore, many parents experience a bit of an identity crisis when their children leave home. “It can provoke questions such as, ‘Who am I? What should I do with my time now?’ It’s a big shift.” 5. Loneliness “It’s wonderful to see children moving on and progressing, but it can make parents feel left behind or feel like they are not part of their child’s new world,” she says. “As their child steps into their new social life and immerses themselves into university life, parents are forced to take a back seat.” This can be particularly challenging for single parents. “If you are going through this alone as a single parent, those feelings of loneliness and loss can feel even more heightened because now it’s just you left in the house,” Wakeland says. Helpful tips If you are struggling to navigate this transition, here are some tips that could help. Be kind to yourself “It’s really normal to feel like this and it’s OK to feel happy and sad at the prospect of your children moving on,” Wakeland says. “The emotions will change and fluctuate, so don’t be too hard on yourself about it. Just allow yourself to feel those emotions and try to be kind and compassionate towards yourself and accept that this is a difficult time.” Pursue new or revisit old interests “Think about what you want your identity to look like now,” Wakeland says. “For example, are there things that you sacrificed before that you could perhaps do now? news_items.title_en: Obama blasts Trump’s ‘chaos and cruelty’ while campaigning for Democrats | South China Morning Post
news_items.summary_en: The former US president slammed his successor’s ‘corruption and incompetence’ and blamed his ‘bad decisions’ for the rising cost of living.
news_items.body: Former US president Barack Obama delivered a scathing critique of his successor, Donald Trump, at a rally in Ohio on Saturday to support Democratic candidates ahead of the November 3 midterm elections. “After two years of chaos and cruelty and corruption and incompetence, the likes of which we have not seen in the modern era, you get a chance to say, ‘Enough is enough,’” Obama declared in Cleveland. “We are voting for change right here in Ohio.” The 65-year-old Democrat blamed the Trump administration for the rising cost of living, a top voter concern amid soaring fuel prices. “The current president chose to make a series of bad decisions,” Obama said. “Most importantly, he decided to start an unnecessary war that nobody asked for.” He noted that instead of lowering costs, the president has instead focused on building a new White House ballroom and helipad on the South Lawn. “I don’t know if you’ve noticed, but he seems very focused on home renovation,” Obama said. “He should be on HGTV.” He went on: “There’s gold everywhere. He’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory.” Obama also urged voters to cast their ballots as soon as possible since early voting is already open in this northern industrial state. “Don’t procrastinate, don’t equivocate,” Obama said. The former president retains considerable popularity among the Democratic base, which he is keen to leverage to support his party’s candidates in the crucial coming elections that will decide control of Congress. In Ohio, former Democratic senator Sherrod Brown will attempt a comeback against incumbent Republican Senator Jon Husted, while the race for governor will be contested between Democrat Amy Acton and Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, a former presidential candidate in 2024. Polls for Ohio give Democrats a slight lead in both those races, but the results are expected to be close. Nationally, polls also suggest that Democrats could regain control of the House of Representatives but face a much more competitive contest for the Senate. After Cleveland, Obama will head north to Michigan this evening for a rally in Detroit alongside Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate candidate. While both of Michigan’s Senate seats are currently held by Democrats, El-Sayed, from the party’s left wing, is in a close race with Republican Mike Rogers. Additional reporting by Associated Press

news_items.title_en: In Focus | China’s next generation of leaders waiting in the wings for more senior roles | South China Morning Post
news_items.summary_en: A meeting in Beijing this week will lay the groundwork for members of the Communist Party’s seventh generation – or 7G – to take on key roles.
news_items.body: Plenary sessions of the Central Committee, the upper echelon of China’s ruling Communist Party, are major events on the country’s political calendar. In the fourth part of this series, William Zheng looks at how the next generation of the party is being formed. When China’s political elites gather behind closed doors in Beijing for the Communist Party’s fifth plenum on Monday, much of the attention will be on the quiet preparations for allocating hundreds of pivotal roles in next year’s 21st party congress. At the heart of this transition is the rise of the party’s seventh generation – often referred to as the 7G – who were born in the late 1960s and the 1970s and whose ascent will be critical in shaping China’s political trajectory. Xie Maosong, a senior researcher at Tsinghua University’s National Institute of Strategic Studies, said the party was looking for cadres who had “absolute political loyalty, integrity, fighting spirit, technological or ‘hard science’ expertise, grass-roots experience and hardship resilience”. “Just like their predecessors, they must demonstrate unquestioned loyalty and integrity. But given China’s technological advancement into uncharted areas, the new leaders will have to know emerging technology and hard science as China can no longer copy from others.” However, recent patterns within the party suggest that Beijing is giving age less weight when it comes to promotions, while the far-reaching anti-corruption campaign is hitting this generation as hard as any other. The 7G Regardless of whether Xi Jinping, now 73, chooses to stay in charge beyond the 2032 party congress, he will still need a deep bench of loyal and talented younger officials to carry out his policies. In recent decades, candidates for Politburo seats have usually been identified many years ahead. Most candidates for membership of the key decision-making body in 2032 will currently be members of the party’s Central Committee or will be selected as alternate members at next year’s party congress. Traditionally, most Central Committee members, who have a ministerial-level rank, are required to step down at the age of 65. Meanwhile, Politburo members observe an informal rule known as “seven up, eight down”, in which those under the age of 67 may serve another five-year term, while those aged 68 or older must retire. Xi broke these precedents for some key figures in 2022, including top diplomat Wang Yi, then aged 69, who was seen as indispensable for managing China’s foreign relations amid escalating competition with the United States. He also kept the country’s top general Zhang Youxia, then aged 72, in place to manage the country’s military modernisation programme, but Zhang later fell from favour and was detained earlier this year on suspicion of corruption. Roughly two-thirds of the current Central Committee will have reached the statutory retirement age by the time of the party congress in October next year. Consequently, the seventh generation, currently about 8 per cent of the party’s central leadership body, is expected to become the biggest cohort. Only 7G officials who are already members of the Central Committee or those who have been newly appointed as ministers and provincial leaders – who will get their Central Committee seat in 2027 – are likely candidates for leadership roles beyond 2032. The leading candidates Some of these contenders have already taken over top regional and ministerial roles this year. They include Zhu Zhongming, born in April 1972, who was appointed as mayor of Shanghai late last month, a role that puts him in line to become the city’s next party chief. Zhu, 54, is a career finance official who spent much of his working life in his native province of Zhejiang, where he worked under Premier Li Qiang while he was governor. Other regional government chiefs of a similar age include Zhejiang governor Liu Jie, Jiangsu governor Liu Xiaotao, and Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region’s government chairman Wei Tao

news_items.title_en: Trump, a critic of early voting, votes early in Florida | South China Morning Post
news_items.summary_en: The US president has reversed course on the practice, hoping to mobilise his base to help Republicans keep control of Congress.
news_items.body: US President Donald Trump cast his ballot for the midterm elections in Palm Beach on Saturday, opting to vote early in his adopted home state of Florida. At rallies ahead of Election Day on November 3, Trump has been urging Republicans to cast their ballots early, reversing course on a practice he has long decried in a bid to mobilise the party’s base in an election that threatens to end their control of Congress. Asked by reporters if he voted for the party line, he said: “Very much so.” The president has regularly questioned the security of early voting methods, claiming without evidence that mail-in ballots, drop boxes and other practices during the 2020 presidential election – which he lost – were used to rig the vote. He has also called for one-day, in-person voting on Election Day. “The US attorney found potentially hundreds of thousands of illicit votes,” Trump told reporters. Earlier this month, the US Justice Department sued California for allegedly failing to join an effort to verify the status of 20,000 suspected non-citizens to prevent any fraudulent ballots from being counted. California asked a judge to deny the request to set aside those 20,000 mail-in ballots, calling the US allegations “a reckless political stunt”. Trump has long amplified false claims of widespread voter fraud in the 2020 election and since his return to the White House last year has taken steps to increase federal control of US elections. The administration has pushed to curb mail-in voting, a method Trump has used in the past. And he has pressured lawmakers to pass legislation that would require voters to have government-issued ID or other proof of citizenship to cast ballots. Senate Republican leaders have said the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility (Save) America Act lacks the support to pass. Trump has spent the better part of October criss-crossing the country to boost Republican candidates as the party faces the challenging task of retaining both the House and Senate in a midterm year. During Florida’s August 2026 primary, Trump cast a ballot by mail. He also said he voted by mail earlier this year in a Florida special election. As a presidential candidate in 2024, he voted in person on Election Day.

The next day, Elon Musk promised one SpaceX share, next year, for “every kid in America” – about US$10.6 billion for some 73 million children. The offers differ in who holds the shares. Anthropic’s will sit in an entity the company owns, spent on the public’s behalf; Musk’s would land, by a route he has not explained, in a child’s name. Should the public own the companies AI makes rich? Silicon Valley has begun answering yes, on its own terms. She spoke in Bangkok; Asia is where economic growth has long depended on creating jobs. America shares growth through wages too, but 62 per cent of adults also own shares. For six decades, Asia’s growth reached households chiefly through the pay packet. Japan’s shunto, the annual wage negotiations between unions and employers, carried prime minister Hayato Ikeda’s 1960 pledge to double national income in a decade; the economy did it in seven years. South Korea’s factories provided wages, and the 1987 strikes gave workers a bigger share. Beijing smashed the iron rice bowl and let private factories absorb the laid-off. Singapore took another route: the state turned wages into housing wealth through compulsory savings and public housing, and during the 2001 slump handed citizens economic-growth-linked New Singapore Shares. Then pay stopped keeping pace. Since the mid-1990s, Japan’s labour ministry calculates, a 1 per cent rise in productivity has lifted wages by about 0.4 per cent, against roughly 1 per cent in America: higher productivity without higher pay, decades before AI. Past automation replaced hands on the factory floor while adding jobs above them. AI now threatens the route where it is weakest. Stanford economists using American payroll data find that employment of those aged 22-25 in the most AI-exposed occupations has fallen by 19 per cent behind the trajectory of less exposed peers, up from 15 per cent a year earlier. Causation is contested and total employment has not fallen. But the pressure is falling first on the young. The newest round of the old bargain was fought this year in Icheon, in South Korea’s Gyeonggi province. SK Hynix, riding on demand for AI chips, agreed last year to hand staff 10 per cent of its operating profit: about 700 million won (US$527,500) a head if this year’s 250 trillion won profit forecast holds. This August, union members voted down a tentative deal to take 60 per cent in shares, wary of a volatile stock and the tax bill. Last month, they settled on half cash, half shares, with the option of more stock. Even the workers closest to the AI boom haggled over how much of their dividend should be in payroll. They are the lucky ones. Last year, 450,000 young Koreans said they wanted no job at all, up from 287,000 in 2019, according to Bank of Korea. Beijing meets a record 12.7 million graduates this year with an “employment first” plan, though a China Daily commentary concedes AI may hit the young first. news_items.title_en: German man detained after fire wrecks Hitler’s ‘Eagle’s Nest’ mountain retreat | South China Morning Post
news_items.summary_en: Firefighters battled to put out flames at the former guest house for top Nazi officials, high up in the Bavarian Alps.
news_items.body: Firefighters battled on Saturday to put out flames that tore through Adolf Hitler’s “Eagle’s Nest” mountain retreat while police detained a suspect who investigators said may have psychiatric problems. The alarm was raised late on Friday at the former guest house for top Nazi officials, 1,834 metres (6,000 feet) high in the Bavarian Alps. As snow fell on the Alpine peak, the Eagle’s Nest was still engulfed in flames at dawn on Saturday, and fire chief Michael Brandl told a press conference the last elements of the inferno were being put out during the afternoon. No one has entered the building because of fears it could collapse, Brandl added. “We are very lucky that there are no injuries,” Brandl said. Some 200 firefighters were mobilised for the operation at the Kehlsteinhaus residence on a summit above Obersalzberg in southern Germany that draws some 350,000 visitors a year, according to Bavarian state authorities. Authorities said access had been difficult after the fire alarm went off at 9.50pm. Heavy rain was followed by a snowstorm and then violent winds hit the mountains. Police spokeswoman Lisa Maier said the firefighters had needed breathing apparatus to get near. Firefighters saw flames rising high into the air as they approached the scene, only to find the building “completely ablaze”, police said. Bavarian state interior minister Joachim Herrmann said the fire appeared to be “a malicious act” and police said that a suspect was detained at the scene. Firefighters and police heading to the Eagle’s Nest saw “a rider on a red motorcycle with no licence plate” and stopped him, Robert Holzinger, a Bavarian police official, told a press conference. The suspect is a 33-year-old German who has ties to the area but does not live there, Rainer Vietze, a public prosecutor’s spokesman, was quoted as saying by the local PNP newspaper. Possible political motives were being examined but investigators believed there was a “potential mental illness”, the spokesman added. Police blocked access to the retreat on Saturday. Built between 1937 and 1938, the Eagle’s Nest forms part of the toxic legacy of Hitler’s Third Reich, which was responsible for the deaths of millions of Jews, Roma, LGBTQ people and Communists during the Holocaust. It was designed to serve as a monument to Hitler’s rule, although the dictator himself seldom visited the complex that was heavily guarded. Hitler had another country residence nearby at Berghof. Built of stone and granite, the Eagle’s Nest offers an exceptional view of the Alpine landscape and was designed to impress foreign diplomats. Hitler used it as a backdrop for his propaganda films. It survived World War II undamaged and later gained notoriety through post-war Hollywood films that recreated the residence. Since 1952, it has hosted both an exhibition recounting the house’s Nazi history and a restaurant. The website says the Eagle’s Nest “stands for the insanity of the regime and the world on the Obersalzberg, where plans for war and mass murder were formed”. The Bavarian interior minister said the retreat “will under no circumstances be left in a state of ruin”. “This house – the entire site and its surroundings – is linked to a specific history. It is important that we continue our work of remembrance,” Herrmann said.

news_items.title_en: China’s J-20 stealth jet designers plan to put powerful radar into aircraft wing | South China Morning Post
news_items.summary_en: Military aircraft designers propose a wing-mounted early-warning radar to expand coverage during air combat.
news_items.body: Fighter jets typically house their main radars behind a radome in the nose, while conventional airborne early-warning aircraft often carry large radar arrays in prominent structures above the fuselage. Although aircraft wings offer a large surface area, their relatively thin cross-sections leave limited internal space for radar equipment. Top Chinese military aircraft designers have now proposed a revolutionary method to integrate large antenna arrays into aircraft wings, using flight manoeuvres and coordinated formations of unmanned aircraft to expand radar coverage. The design was outlined in a study published online on October 10 in the peer-reviewed Chinese journal Measurement & Control Technology, which presented wing-mounted radar as a new approach to building multifunctional, high-performance airborne early-warning systems. “Wing-mounted early-warning radar is a new type of mission payload designed to meet the early-warning needs of distributed air combat,” researcher Ren Yunsong and his team wrote, describing the concept as “a new pathway” to developing systems with strong detection capabilities. Ren and his team are affiliated with AVIC Chengdu Aircraft Design and Research Institute, which developed China’s J-20 stealth fighter and was identified by the country’s defence ministry as the designer of the two-seat J-20S, a variant intended to operate alongside unmanned aircraft. The concept builds on distributed air combat, a strategic idea first proposed by the US Defence Advanced Research Projects Agency or Darpa in 2014 to explore future air warfare. The researchers argued that this approach could not rely solely on conventional early-warning aircraft, which use large radar arrays and high-power systems, but would instead require numerous smaller, lower-cost unmanned aircraft to work together to provide surveillance. This creates a technical challenge: achieving large-scale detection capabilities with relatively small individual platforms. The proposed design integrates the antenna array, control components and associated systems within the wing structure, with the radiating surface facing downwards and a protective cover following the aircraft’s outer contours, increasing the available antenna aperture without requiring a large external radar dome. To direct the radar towards different sectors, the researchers propose changing the aircraft’s flight attitude. In the proposed side-flying mode, an unmanned aircraft rolls at an angle of more than 45 degrees, tilting the wing-mounted array from a downward-facing position towards the side. “By adjusting the drone’s flight attitude, the radar beam can be dynamically controlled, expanding the airspace covered by early warning,” Ren wrote. The design is intended to support distributed airborne early-warning operations, in which multiple smaller unmanned aircraft share surveillance duties rather than relying on a single large platform. “The research provides a reusable and verifiable design paradigm for the engineering implementation of wing warning radars and has a promising application prospect and promotion value,” Ren’s team wrote. The paper proposes four operating modes, including all-direction and multi-direction detection, as well as coordinated operations in which aircraft provide wide-area coverage, concentrate on specific targets or work together to counter electronic interference. “Cooperative detection by multiple aircraft is a core enabling technology for the operational concept of ‘small platforms, big capabilities’,” it said. The researchers said the approach could provide early-warning capabilities approaching or exceeding those of conventional early-warning aircraft without relying on large platforms. Ren said the design would provide a solid information-sensing foundation for distributed air combat involving next-generation aircraft. The concept could potentially be considered for future Chinese combat aircraft, including the J-20 and next-generation designs

news_items.title_en: Longevity-first healthcare takes spotlight at Abu Dhabi Future Health Summit | South China Morning Post
news_items.summary_en: The event explores innovative breakthroughs and policies emphasising prediction and prevention to help people lead longer, healthier lives.
news_items.body: Issues affecting ageing populations worldwide will form the core of discussions for policymakers and health industry leaders gathered at the Abu Dhabi Future Health Summit, with a particular emphasis on how practising prediction and prevention can help ensure life is lived to its fullest. The United Arab Emirates (UAE) has positioned itself as a global leader in transformative healthcare policy, and Dr Asma Al Mannaei, executive director of the health life science sector at the Department of Health – Abu Dhabi, regards the summit as an opportunity to share how those policies are playing out in real time. “Precision medicine is at the heart of it,” Al Mannaei explains, adding that the key to ensuring better health is “understanding each person’s risk through their genome, their biomarkers and their daily life, then acting early.” The Abu Dhabi Future Health Summit is the flagship event of the Future Health platform, the UAE capital’s year-round initiative to promote global collaboration and transformative health innovation. The stated goal of the summit is to shape a future where innovation and collaboration come together “to enable longer, healthier lives for all”. Much of the summit will be focused on the world’s ageing populations – a common denominator between contemporary societies, with the World Health Organization estimating that by 2050, there will be more than 2 billion people aged over 60 across the globe. This statistic has not only drawn more attention to the issue of how to care for people as they age, but Al Mannaei also points out that it has created a need to design entire health systems focused on ensuring the advancing years are spent in as much good health as possible. “Every health system faces the same question: will those added years be healthy years? Our answer is to invest now in prediction and prevention,” she says. “Our model has four steps: we sense, we predict, we prevent and we personalise. We sense through genomics, screening and data. We predict risk years before the symptoms appear. And we prevent through early targeted intervention.” Among Abu Dhabi’s success stories is the Emirati Genome Programme (EGP), launched across the UAE in 2019 with a target of mapping the genetic make-up of all Emiratis. To date, more than 800,000 records have been collected. Al Mannaei says the idea behind the programme is that knowing an individual’s genetic make-up can help establish a “foundation for precision prevention”. Already, the EGP data has proved revelatory. For example, it revealed that within the Emirati population, there are around 100 genetic factors associated with inherited vision loss. Other initiatives include Malaffi, the region’s first health information exchange that is a strategic initiative of the Department of Health – Abu Dhabi. Launched in 2019 and operated by Abu Dhabi Health Data Services, Malaffi connects more than 3,000 healthcare facilities and brings together over 4 billion records for more than 14 million patients. “It gives clinicians secure access to patients’ comprehensive health records, supporting continuity of care, patient safety and better-informed clinical decisions,” Al Mannaei says. “In Abu Dhabi, policy, regulation, care delivery, research, technology and investment move together around one vision,” she notes. “When we built the Emirati Genome Programme, we built the governance, the data, the infrastructure and the partnership at the same time. That let discovery move into care and into the economy at speed.” Al Mannaei adds: “I hope Abu Dhabi will be known as the place that proved a longevity-first health system works. It will be the blueprint of how health systems can sense, predict, prevent and personalise, helping people everywhere live longer, healthier and more fulfilling lives.” Watch the video for more insights from Dr Asma Al Mannaei about Abu Dhabi’s role in advancing healthcare focused on longevity.
